title: Oliver at the Royal Garden, Armstrong's arrival and 35th Street
summary: He follows the Royal Garden bands, Oliver's move to Dave Peyton after the fire, Armstrong's arrival, and the cabarets along State and 35th Street.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: He had the band. Yeah, I couldn't call his name just then. Yeah. And then right across the street was Joe Oliver played over there. Holly Powers did the singing. Joe was doubling, he was doubling at the Pekin. He'd leave the Dreamland and go to Pekin. And then later, at that time now, this Royal Garden, this is when I first saw, I saw Emmanuel Perez here, but this Paul Barber, he was playing drums with this band. And it was Bill Johnson's band, bass player, who lived to be a hundred years old, died, I think it was last year. And so they had Emmanuel and Freddie, Freddie Kevick, Jimmy Newman, and they had Eddie Vincent. And there was a woman playing piano by the name of Lottie Taylor. And Bill Johnson was on the bass. That was the person that was this band. Well, it seemed like they lost out there in time. And the next thing I knew, Joe Oliver had the band over there. And you know, his person there was Joe Dutre and Baby Dots and Johnny Dots. And he had Lil on the piano. And Bill on the same, Bill Johnson played bass with him. So that was the person that loved that band during that time.
What about have the Lottie Taylor? Oh, Lottie Taylor?
Well, I guess she passed. It's like the rest of a lot of people. She never been married.

Well, I never did know whether she could have been married then as far as I knew. Yeah. But Joe had several women pianists. It seemed like there was more women pianists who played that type of music than the men. Now there was a pianist up there from here called Arthur Campbell too. He played with George Field in the spot. And later on, fellas like Tom Aladdin came up and Mutt was up there for a while. And they came up, I think Mary Mack, like Mary Mack had, they played at the Monogram Theater. And so they began to, I missed the music, you know, at the beginning until I found out where this different band was. And so I said, well, this is just like New Orleans. I mean, we used to just ramble all night there. We'd go to like a place called the Funky London. And a few of those from then, it's like Bourbon Street. A few of those from there was the dream. And just died and right across the street on the corner, Deluxe. And then you'd keep on State Street and you didn't. He liked number one, he liked number two. And by the time you hit 31st Street then you'd, the place is called Schiller's, this band, this jazz band from Memphis. I think the Memphis Fire plays was playing there then. And so then you'd go on the road, Royal Gardens, Joe was the band. And so that was it. I mean, later on they, later on Joe, when he left there, they changed the name of the place to the Lincoln Gardens. And I was supposed to go to WIC, take the George Fields place. But the place caught on fire Christmas Eve. They changed it from the Royal Gardens to the Lincoln Gardens. And so that made Joe out of jobs. And so Joe went to work with Dave Payton, who later on I worked in this band too. But Joe was only there a short time. Joe was a pretty good businessman. I can't understand why he went down so rapid. But I understand too that it was pyreia, you know. And he never was the same. And he never did come back to me. He was close in the order of him to come back, you know. Like Shreveport and places like that he was band. When I was with Louis Armstrong, we met him in Galveston. But he never did come back. And Freda didn't either. He never did come back to me. So it wasn't long before Joe had his own band at the plantation. Now the plantation would be like he hadn't died or the Red Cross, it was the sunset. And Red Cross Street was the nest. And Jimmy Noon, he would play the 12 o'clock with Dr. Cook's 26 piece band. And then he would have his own band, Earl Hines and Bud Scott and Lawson Buford. I forgot, Johnny Wells drums, yeah. And so in time, Louis went to work. I saw Louis the first when he arrived. I was sitting on the stand. I knew he was coming because I heard Joe, I always say that Brother Dick would be here soon. So true enough, the night he was supposed to come, he did come. And I was sitting on the stand. I'll never forget he had on a sail over the Brownsuit, tan shoes, you know. And he came and he started the very next night. Well, it wasn't long before he set that time on fire. And he stayed there for about two years. So finally he had an offer to join Fletcher Henderson. So he went to New York, he stayed there a year with Fletcher Henderson. He was coming back and joined his wife, Lil. By that time she had the band at the Dreamland. So he went from the Dreamland with Tate at the Vendome. Tate had an orchestra that, at Shellow and instruments like that, about three fields. They played a lot of overtures but they featured Armstrong, you know, and the hot stuff. And he doubled from there to the Sunset with Carol Dickinson's band. So Joe Glazer had the, that was his mother's place, he was running the place. And I'd say the manager, or the boss if you want to call it. And so he and Carol had some woods. So he fired Carol and I saw Lewis come to have the band. So they're shooting at one another all night long. He and Joe, obviously. Yeah, and it was something to see. The place, even back to the Royal Garden about the first ten rows, musician Husker would have. And Paul Morales was there, you know, his band, New Orleans, Little King. And all that, I would say around one o'clock. There was four or five bands there. There was Miff Moe that came down to Venuti and all those bands. They'd come away, we'd have a little vacation, come from far away to New York. And that's where I first saw the Dorset Brothers and one of my favorite trombones, Jack Teagarden. And this boy wrote the similar blues, the Bix. Yeah, they all were there, see, all were there. And Joe Oliver. And then when they moved a few blocks farther south, well, they continued to come around Bing Crawl and all that bunch. You could see them every night. And all up and down 35th night, George Field had a band. And then Tommy Ladner had a band on 35th Street. 35th was just loaded just like Bourbon Street. And they had the entertainers, John Wycliffe had the band of entertainers. And so it just was, some guys had two jobs. Everybody that wanted to work could play great. And some of them had two jobs.
